blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A composite variable is a single score built by combining several items or indicators, intended to represent a construct more completely than any single item.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Once internal consistency (§16.3.1.1) and dimensionality (§16.5) have been checked, item responses are combined into one score. That score is the variable used in the substantive analysis.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A 10-item satisfaction scale with acceptable α and one dominant component becomes a satisfaction score for each patient: the sum or mean of the items. It then becomes the outcome when mean satisfaction is compared between two PHCs.

points.html: The simplest composite is an unweighted sum or mean, giving every item equal weight.

A weighted composite uses the component or factor weights, so items with higher loadings count more. An asset-based wealth index is built this way, with weights from PCA (Filmer & Pritchett, 2001; §16.5).
The proper order is: content validity at design; collect data; check internal consistency and dimensionality; then build the composite; then assess criterion and construct validity.

A sum of ordinal items is often treated as approximately continuous in later analysis. This is a working approximation, not a promotion to an interval scale (recall §1.1.2). Whether it is reasonable depends on the measurement model, the items, the dimensionality and the validation evidence, not on the arithmetic of adding.
